utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There were two items still on our list where the Defence would have to inform the Chamber, which was impossible yesterday, that is, about the scheduling of the remainder of the case and report on expert witnesses. Meanwhile, the Chamber has received some information. The first one is that the Defence will -- has reviewed the witness list and that you have decided not to call 30 witnesses. And then it says the time saved for not calling these witnesses will be reallocated to remaining witnesses. I do understand that that is the way in which you would like to use your time. The Chamber will further consider this. We do not have yet the names of the witnesses, which ones are -- do you have the list of 30, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It can be provided to Your Honours during the day. I don't have it with me, but I know that on Sunday we discussed and we specifically marked whom we are not going to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have a final list of that, of course, the Chamber would appreciate to know which ones are stricken because we are, of course, working on the basis of our witness list and our 65 ter summaries. That is one issue. Again, about how to use the time, we might need to analyse a bit more in detail what happened until now in terms of time, not the ultimate number of hours used but also how they were used, but we'll further analyse that before we -- we express ourselves on which we would expect the Defence to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, as you know, we do not have that many 92 ter witnesses left, so in the future we will be using time much more than we did until now, since we have to lead some witnesses viva voce and we will spend much more time with each witness in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at your -- at time estimates and which witnesses will be stricken, and then we'll look at the whole of it and then we'll give further guidance or even perhaps further instructions to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there no 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There will be some 92 bis witnesses, but I don't think more than 10, I think, 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number is quite limited from what I remember from your original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, again, we'd like to hear from you further details about witnesses you have taken out and could you please do that in writing rather than to read long lists of names in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we also received - and there was a deadline for that as well - some information about expert witnesses. Well, it's only for three expert witnesses that you announce in more detail what you expect will happen, that is, that the reports will be there the first two weeks of February. All the rest is rather vague, what you hope, and you're going to update. Well, that doesn't give really the information, I think, we were seeking in sufficient detail. So therefore, we received it only yesterday evening, late, we have not discussed it yet. But if there's anything can you add to what is found in that e-mail which says that demographer Svetlana Radovanovic, military expert Mitar Kovac, and demolition of cultural sites expert Dragic Gojkovic were -- are expected to have the reports ready and for you to be filed in the first two weeks in February. And that for the two ballistic experts, that they are being prepared and that you hopefully soon will be in a position to know when their 94 bis admission will be expected to be filed. And finally, the radio communications expert and history expert and forensic pathologist, that you asked them for an update. Of course, the Chamber asked you for an update rather than to hear from you that you passed on this request. I just summarised what we found in the e-mail exchange so that this -- so that it is on the record. The Chamber certainly will insist on receiving rather soon far more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we may set a deadline for that. We'll consider that once we have discussed your e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on to another item on my agenda, which is the Defence Rule 92 ter motion for Milan Tutoric. On the 19th of November, the -- of last year, the Defence filed a motion to have the evidence of Witness Milan Tutoric be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter. On the 3rd of December, the Prosecution filed its response objecting to the admission of the evidence on the ground that, inter alia, the written statement: 1, contains inadmissible opinion evidence; and, 2, lacks relevance and fails to meet the minimum threshold of reliability. The Prosecution further objects to the introduction of an expert opinion from this witness who is presented by the Defence as a witness of fact. On 18th of December, the Chamber expressed a desire for the Defence to file an additional submission addressing whether it would be more appropriate for the Defence to introduce this witness as an expert witness. The Chamber set a deadline of the 12th of January of this year for this submission. As of today's date, the Defence has not filed or presented an additional submission, and under these circumstances the Chamber denies, without prejudice, the Defence motion pursuant to Rule 92 ter to admit the written testimony of Milan Tutoric. Although I have a few more items on my agenda, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I just complained to Registry this morning that it was very hard for us to track all the deadlines and the decisions, and we are -- as you would notice lately, we missed several deadlines and it was the reason why, because we cannot track all the decisions. So I would kindly ask you to give us with Milan Tutoric more time. I was of an opinion that even that motion is filed to have him as an expert witness, so I don't know what happened. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to regroup after this break because we just gathered here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the problems, Mr. Lukic, is that the interlocutory decision has been delivered a minute ago by me, and we can't just immediately undo that. If anything was filed, we'll see it, but we'll consider the whole situation, and that we said "without prejudice," which is part of our decision, means that you have an opportunity with new arguments to re-open the debate. We'll see what comes. But granting additional time after we've delivered our decision is not something that is easily done. If you would have asked us to reconsider it, then we would still need reasons for that. But if the decision is given without prejudice, then, of course, you don't even -- I would say if you have good arguments, you can re-introduce the matter, and there's no reason for us to reconsider the decision because you can introduce the matter again --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on better grounds. Finally, if you have difficulties in tracking deadlines, there is a very simple solution for that; that is, to organise yourself, make a spreadsheet, and everyone who hears of a deadline in court, counsel, writes it down. It will be imported in the spreadsheet immediately after which can you sort on date, on names, on kind of -- it's really not that complex. It makes the Chamber fear that the deadlines we set were not accurately recorded within your own system, which is worrying. I think that for the witness, Mr. Zoric, you still have some time left, I think some 15 minutes, for examination-in-chief. Are you ready to continue, Mr. Stojanovic? Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can briefly deal with one matter. That is a matter remaining with the testimony of Milos Skrba. During the testimony of Witness Skrba in June 2014, the Chamber asked -- I'll stop because otherwise the witness would have to wait too long. I'll re-visit the scale of maps issue soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue to hear your evidence, but before we do so, I'd like to remind that you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue. Could you perhaps go a little bit further away from the microphone. Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. With your leave, I would like to read a brief summary of this witness's statement. I believe that's where we left off with the questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Milorad Zoric is a defectologist by training, and until the war, he worked as an educator in Bihac. That's where he was when the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He testifies about the deterioration of inter-ethnic relations, the arming of Muslims in Bihac, and attacks on JNA barracks in Bihac. He was forced to leave the town on 25 May 1992, and immediately after his leaving, his apartment was broken into by six armed persons. After leaving town, he joined the VRS which took him in, fed him, and gave him clothing after which he was assigned to the 15th Bihac Light Infantry Brigade. One month later, he was transferred to the press centre of the 2nd Krajina Corps. He stayed there until the end of the war, working as a war cameraman, doing jobs for the corps, for the Serbian TV, and the Reuters agency. Further on in his statement, he says that without encountering any problems or restrictions, he followed and filmed a large number of important events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including visits by General McKenzie, Mr. Clark, General Morillon, Mr. Akashi and others. He followed and filmed also assembly meetings and toured front lines and the sites of numerous battles. He made about 500 exclusive reports that were sent by -- to Reuters and picked up by other world agencies. He says that he noticed that news from Republika Srpska were unable to breakthrough the media blockade that had been imposed on Republika Srpska. The witness personally filmed a large number of locations and victims of Serb nationality who were visibly mutilated at exchanges and territories that were burnt down, causing rage and desire for vengeance on the Serbian side. He speaks about a large number of encounters with General Mladic during the war and the interviews that he had with him. He describes in detail the positions held by General Mladic on the war, the objectives of the war, honouring of the enemy, asking this reporter to publish only the truth. That is all. With your leave, I would like to put only three questions to this witness to clarify his statement. Could we call up in e-court, please, a document which is now D877, paragraph 14, and that is the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zoric, in a minute you will see the text of your statement. Please focus on paragraph 14 where you mentioned the fact that on 24 May 1992, a day before you left Bihac, you went to see a friend at the assembly building where she worked that evening. Could you please tell the Court why you emphasised this, this meeting you had that evening in the building of the assembly of the municipality of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that. That friend is a lady with whom I lived in a common-law marriage. She worked in the municipality of Bihac, and at that time all enterprises and businesses were organising night-time duty service. So she asked me to visit her at work that evening. The time -- the town was calm and peaceful. And when I got there, she was waiting for me. A shoot-out started, a skirmish. I can't say exactly from where the shooting was coming, but I believe all the sides were -- both sides were shooting. From the centre, you can't really see where the shooting is coming from. Panic broke out. Some of the clerks who were former schoolmates of mine with whom I had grown up and had no discrimination whatsoever against them were starting to shout at me: Look what your people are doing to us, et cetera et cetera. I left quickly and went to the apartment of my sister at the other end of town. My sister was married to a Muslim, and I felt sort of safer with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why you decided to leave Bihac and your home?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very hard in Bihac during those last days, especially when you leave your house. People were shouting at you: We should chase you out; you should be killed. I wasn't used to hearing such threats. I'm a peaceful man by nature. I had never thought that this time would come for us to part ways. I decided to leave town with my lady friend. She decided to leave the town and her family behind. On 25 May, we got into the car and just left. If you want me, I can tell you the details of that departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. Let's look at paragraph 26 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D877 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, you talk about how impossible it was to break through the media blockade in Republika Srpska. Could you please tell the Court why you mentioned that your statement, why you believed that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once the war had started, when both sides took up military positions, one man came from the United States, a Serb immigrant to the United States, he brought some aid for our fighters, and he asked me to make a compilation of all the recordings, all the films I had made. So I gathered whatever I could from other TV stations and films that I made myself. He said - and he lived in New Jersey - I'll try to take it to the United States. And later he found me and said: Not a single TV station wants to broadcast this, no matter how much money I offered. So there was a media blockade. The first news from our side started to come out when the Reuters agency established themselves in Republika Srpska. They published and broadcast quite correct reporting about our side. That was in 1994 and later. From that time on, it was easier to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 of your statement, D877. Mr. Zoric, just for clarification, tell the Court about this last interview you had with General Ratko Mladic. Where did it take place? Where did you speak with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is indeed the last interview he gave. It was in the beginning of August at the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps at Ostrelj, that's between Drvar and Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, thank you very much for answering our questions on behalf of the Defence team of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just put one question for clarification. You just said it was in the beginning of August, but in your statement it says at the end of August 1995. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we amended this statement. It was the beginning of August. Together with the lawyer, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, during the proofing we corrected this. And thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to just discuss briefly your -- the units that were in and your commanding officers. Now, in your statement we read that after your mobilisation on the 9th of May, 1992, you were assigned to the 15th Bihac Light Infantry Brigade. Now, at this time, your brigade commander was Sveto Mrdja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was Colonel Matic. Sveto Mrdja came later, after Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you know when that change in command took place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't interested. But in practice, soldiers do know when such changes take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now we also read in your statement that in June 1992, you were transferred to the press centre of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Now at this time, the 2nd Krajina Corps commander was Major-General Grujo Boric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was later succeeded in November 1994 by Major-General Radivoje Tomanic. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomanic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you remained a member of the 2nd Krajina press corps throughout the war from June 1992 onwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2nd Corps from June onwards, and in the VRS from 9 May 1992 to 31st March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And within the 2nd Corps from June onwards, you were a member of the 2nd Krajina Corps press centre until the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 22 of your statement, you refer to yourself as a journalist of Reuters. Now I understand by that, that you mean that as a member of the 2nd Krajina press centre you would occasionally supply material to Reuters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. With the permission of my superiors. Sometimes I didn't even ask for permission. I did whatever I thought was needed, whatever I thought was right. Nobody ever had any quarrel with it. Everybody even wanted to see it and they wanted the truth about their work to spread. As for Reuters, a team of the Reuters agency came from Belgrade and spent a month with us. There was a large operation going on at that time, the state of war had been declared, and they had received permission from our top commander, from General Mladic and General Milovanovic, to be there, and they were with me at the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps, without any problem whatsoever. And in order to leave, they engaged me because I was already involved in that work. They hired me to work for them, and I did. But on one condition: That my recordings and my stories go first to our television, the television of Republika Srpska which was then called Banja Luka TV; and after these recordings were broadcast on our TV, they were sent by link to Belgrade. So that big TV was never competing with small TVs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, that's an answer to my question. Now I'd like to move to a different topic, and that is relating to organisation and arming in Bihac during 1991 and 1992. Now in paragraphs 2 to 6 of your statement, you refer to the organising and arming of Muslims in Bihac during 1991 and 1992. Now, can we agree that members of the Serb population in Bihac were also organising and arming during 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for arming, I was in Bihac. I mean, when people felt that something unpleasant would happen -- we didn't believe it would actually be a war. We thought it would not last very long. I often returned to the press centre of the air force in Bihac, that is, at the JNA centre. I felt safer there with the army. The JNA was still there then. It was a guarantor for the constitution and Yugoslavia still existed. I observed all of that, of course, and then I stood by them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. The question is whether you agree that Serbs were arming as well in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but probably yes, both. I mean, I know about these because some officers told me that they had problems with Muslims who want to attack the barracks, to seize weapons, and also there was a black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'd like to show you a document in connection with your answer and maybe we can get a little bit more clarity by looking at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31888 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the screen before you is a report sent from the public security station in Bihac to the CSB in Banja Luka and we can see that it's dated the 13th of October, 1993. Now, as we see from the cover page, it contains information on employees of the Bihac SJB who participated in preparing and organising the Serbian people before the war broke out. And I'd just like to briefly refer your attention to a few parts of this document and then I'll have a couple of questions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2, please, in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, referring your attention to the first sentence of the first paragraph, we read that: "When the war broke out in the territory of Croatia or, to be more precise, in Plitvice on 1 April 1991, the Serbian people in the territory of Bihac municipality instinctively felt the threat posed by the Ustasha and started organising themselves." If we go to the second paragraph and again looking at the first sentence we read: "It was necessary to act in strict secrecy and illegally since many Serbs had been taken in by various political parties and lived in the belief that there would be no war and that the rest of the country would unite in a 'new' Yugoslavia." Looking at the third paragraph, sir, we read in the first sentence: "When the first weapons arrived in the Bihac area, they were unpacked and distributed in great secrecy to civilian protection units which had organised themselves illegally in the Serbian villages in Bihac municipality." And that paragraph goes on to discuss, a few sentences down, arming during the summer of 1991 and also explains that this took place away from the eyes of the public and even individual Serbs. I'd just like to refer you to one other part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3 in the English, please, and page 5 in the B/C/S. And in the English, it's the penultimate paragraph, beginning: "The month of April 1992 ..." And in the B/C/S, it's halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we read: "The month of April 1992 was used to provide the Serbs with additional arms and the special role of the police officers was to provide transport and personally transport weapons. All the approaches to the town were controlled by Muslim police officers, which made the Serbs more afraid. An attempt was made to strike back at the Muslims by setting up check-points manned by Serbian police officers." So, Mr. Zoric, is it your position that you were not aware of the organising and arming of Serbian villages in the Bihac municipality during the course of 1991 and 1992, as we see described in some detail in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took an oath here that I would speak the truth. This document doesn't mean a thing to me. I worked as a teacher in a school in Bihac. I had no idea whatsoever about any of this because I never liked weapons or anything like that. The only thing that I wanted to do was to get my hands on a camera so that I wouldn't have to shoot because I hate that from the bottom of my heart. This is the first time I see this. I know some of the people from this list. I know that they worked somewhere out there, but that that was done, no, I wasn't in these circles. I spent my free time in taverns, at home, in school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether you were not aware. Where you spent your time, whether you know the people in the document, all that was not asked, so I do understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, from your answer, then, I think you'll -- well, do you allow for the possibility that this organising and arming was going on but you simply were not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31888 receives Exhibit Number P7065, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to move to a different topic and that's the topic of population movement. Now, in paragraph 12 of your statement, you refer to Serbs self-organising in Serb villages around Bihac. And you state that the population there relocated in an unorganised and uncontrolled manner. Now I'd like to focus on another municipality bordering the Una river, namely, Bosanska Krupa, which you also discuss in your statement. Now, establishing a border on the Una river was one of the strategic objectives or goals of the Bosnian Serb and political leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishment of the border? I don't know. I was interested in how far I could go to take pictures. I don't know anything else. I wasn't interested in politics. I was just interested in recording what I could report. As for borders, believe me, I had no idea whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this Chamber has received evidence that six strategic goals or objectives were presented by Radovan Karadzic to delegates at the 16th Assembly in Sanski Most on the 12th of May, 1992. Now, was this one of the assembly sessions that you were there recording?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recorded that assembly. We cameramen were allowed to go in, take pictures, see who was there, and finally to wait for the end to see if somebody wanted to give statements to us. Only General Ninkovic wanted to. We stopped General Mladic as well. He was visibly angry. He said: I'm not saying anything. Ask the politicians, they know everything. Then General Ninkovic made a statement. I can't remember it. There's no need for me to remember it, actually. There's a recording of that, so it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, at this session - and the Trial Chamber has received this evidence - a representative of Bosanska Krupa declared that on the right bank of the Una, there were no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. And he went on to state that it was unlikely that those Muslims would have a place to return to now that President Karadzic had told the assembly the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that particular speech?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, I was not present during the assembly meeting. We were waiting outside, waiting for it to finish. This is the first time I hear of this. I have no idea about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now -- but you were in Bosanska Krupa, however, and, in fact, you recorded in the SDA premises there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SDS premises, no. I just took pictures of the positions of combatants along the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, yes, you're recorded as having asked for SDA premises. I don't know why the responded as he did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I know what you mean. I misheard what you said. SDS premises, yes. I got there with my colleagues from the Krupa radio and then they showed us what they had seized from Muslims. We found knives there that they called Serb cutters. Then lists of persons who were supposed to be arrested or killed or whatever. I cannot say. I don't know. And then other small things, equipment for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, so just to confirm, you were present at the SDA premises making these recordings and -- that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that it was the SDA before that. I was never on the Muslim side once the war started. I couldn't go. Didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: What date was this that you -- that you made this film?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in the summer 1992. Now was it June or something like that ... I don't remember the date. After all, it's been more than 20 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, this -- this Chamber has received evidence that on the 22nd of May, 1992, there was an order from the president of the War Presidency in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa to evacuate the remaining Muslim population from that municipality. And that's P7385 [sic]. Is this evacuation of Muslims something that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of May, 1992? I was in Bihac. I mean, I didn't go anywhere. Actually, I didn't even believe that there was conflict in Krupa. I don't know. I wasn't recording anything then either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm going to move to another document in connection with this. I wonder if I should do that now or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how much time you would need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Probably more than three minutes, but not more than five or six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll just go over the 10.30 moment. Please start already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this decision by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I referred to, that the Una river is an indisputable border of Republika Srpska, that was communicated to soldiers of the 2nd Krajina Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just take a look at a document in connection with that, that you might be able to help us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31864.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on your screen you is a war bulletin by the VRS, 2nd Krajina Corps, and it's dated August 1992. Is that a document that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did issue a war bulletin, but I don't remember this particular issue or something. We received communication from all brigades of the corps and then we just put it all together, compiled it, edited it. Actually, I didn't do any of that. It was the journalists who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 25 in the English, please, and 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, we see at the bottom of the page that the document is being -- or we see a reference to the 2nd Krajina Corps Information Service. Now, I take from -- from that it was the 2nd Krajina Corps Information Service responsible for the preparation of this document, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 22 in the English and 13 in the B/C/S. And in the B/C/S I'd like to focus on the text on the right-hand side of the page in -- in the middle, referring to the SRBiH Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, just very quickly, we see a reference to the SRBiH Assembly and we read that the SRBiH has unanimously reached a decision on disputable and indisputable borders of its country, and we see that indisputable borders are -- and we see a reference there to the Una river. Now, sir, this is an example of the 2nd Krajina Corps informing its soldiers about the war aims of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, maybe, but I don't remember that. I wasn't really interested. I had my own work and that's what I did. As for writing, I wasn't really very interested in that. Wasn't interested in politics either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender an excerpt of this document. What I'll suggest is that I create an excerpt of the first page, the last page that we looked at, and this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we should reserve a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The excerpt receives number P7066, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you let us know as soon as you've uploaded the excerpt --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'll do that this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would there be any objection, Mr. Stojanovic? No objection. Therefore, the -- P7066 is admitted into evidence. Although immediately I add to this, that instruction is given to Madam Registrar to upload the excerpt -- to replace the text presently in e-court by the excerpt still to be uploaded, and would you then provide the number once you have uploaded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for planning purposes, I expect to conclude within five to ten minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, as far as the Chamber is aware, no motion was filed this morning in relation to Witness Tutoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zoric, I'd like to conclude today by discussing Bihac and the Bihac safe area. Now, you discuss Bihac in your statement and you refer to your leaving Bihac in May 1992. Now, even at that time there was a shortage of food and medicine in Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, exactly. Shops were empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the next year, in 1993, in May, the United Nations Security Council declared Bihac a safe area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, paragraphs 38 through to 45, you make a series of observations in respect to General Mladic. You mention that he would say the civilian population and especially the weak should be protected, and you conclude the section by saying that he was especially sensitive to old people and children. Now, in respect to Bihac, this Chamber has received evidence that during the course of 1994 and 1995, General Mladic was personally warned by UNPROFOR Generals Cot, de Lapresle, and Smith to stop large-scale attacks on the Bihac safe area. And that's P5186, P5193, and P792. So were you aware of these attacks against the Bihac safe area in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no way of knowing. I wasn't planning attacks or organising anything. I just wanted to have footage that was as attractive as possible and I wanted to record the actual situation as it was. I've already told you, I don't know anything about politics and I was not part of those circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, my question doesn't relate to politics. My question relates to military actions against the safe area of Bihac in 1994 and 1995 and whether you were aware of those.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew partly that Bihac was a safe area but I also have some convincing footage. I mean, I took pictures of weapons, cannons, barrels that are lowered, cows that are grazing around these cannons, so obviously they were not operating for a while. I have all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether you were aware of attacks, not on whether you drew any conclusions on the basis of cows grazing there, but whether you knew anything about the attacks. If not, please say no; if you do have, please tell us what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. I didn't know anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you also say in your statement that you recorded meetings between General Mladic and UNPROFOR officials and you say that General Mladic would request that these meetings be videotaped. That's paragraph 20. Now, this Chamber has received evidence that at one such meeting between General Mladic and UNPROFOR General Rupert Smith in Vlasenica on 7th of March, 1995, when General Mladic was warned that an attack on an UN safe area would risk a response by NATO, he responded with a tirade of threats of counteraction to Mr. Smith -- to General Smith. Now, did you ever record General Mladic threatening UNPROFOR officials in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My area of movement was the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps, and I never recorded anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zoric, the last set of questions after the break related to the fighting around Bihac, the protected area of Bihac. Now, in the context of paragraph 30 of your statement, would you tell the Court if you filmed and documented the attacks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 5th Corps against the VRS from protected areas?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, to the extent I was able to from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court when the attacks from the protected area of Bihac were the most intensive against the positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An offensive was launched towards the end of October from the protected area against the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't remember exactly. They moved in to the territory of the VRS very forcefully and very quickly, including Mount Grmec, 25 kilometres deep into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us around what time and which area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1994, as I said. And the first place they took was the Grabez Plateau that had been held by the VRS; my native village Pritoka, I filmed it as it burned including my own house on fire; and then they went further in the territory of Bihac up to Lipa village. And their aim was to take control of the road towards Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the casualties of that offensive launched from the protected area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a place called Kulen Vakuf, in Rajnovci, in Hrgari and the surrounding areas, especially in Gornji Vakuf [as interpreted], I came across very ugly things, human corpses, carcasses, houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish. My colleague tells me that on the record, page 26, line 19, there is a name of a town. Are you talking about Gornji Vakuf or Kulen Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kulen Vakuf. There are several places in Bosnia called Vakuf but the one I'm talking about, the one closest to Bihac, is called Kulen Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, when you were mentioning the names of the commanding officers and members of the 2nd Krajina Corps, do you recall who was the commander of the staff headquarters at the beginning of the war in 1992 at the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Colonel Mikan Vaso. He occupied the position of assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the staff commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eldar Nikanovic [as interpreted], a native of Tuzla. He came with the army from Sibenik and he's still with the army based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim. It's not Nikanovic. It's Kikanovic, with a K.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just spell out the name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eldar, E-l-d-a-r, Kikanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the behalf of the Defence team of General Mladic, I thank you very much for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have concluded my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When asked about attacks launched against the Bihac safe area, you answered that you had no way of knowing, that you were not planning the attacks or organising anything, that you just wanted to have footage, and that your only focus was on recording what you saw. You further explained that you were not interested in politics and you were not in those circles. Then it was put to you that the question was about military action, and in answer to that observation, you said: "I knew partly that Bihac was a safe area, but I also have some convincing footage. I mean, I took pictures of weapons," and then you continue about that. And then I said -- asked you whether you were aware of attacks rather than about cows. And then you said: "I didn't know. I didn't know anything about that." And that's what we heard you repeatedly say, that whenever it is about -- whether it's arming, whether it's about attacks which, as it was put to you, was committed by Serbs, you claim to have no interest whatsoever in those matters. And as soon as questions are put to you about military action by the Muslims, you immediately, in great detail, tell us what you know about this. Do you have any explanation as to why you are not interested in any military matters and are only interested in getting footage if it is about Serb operations or actions; whereas, to the contrary, if it comes to Muslims' activities or operations, that you expose great interest and detailed knowledge about everything that happened. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every time they attacked, we were afraid that we would come under attack too. I knew enough about the opposite side to be afraid of their attacks, and my job was to film whatever I could and as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You missed the gist of my question. The gist of my question was why you seemed to have detailed knowledge if it is about action and operations against the Serbs; whereas you claim to have no interest and no knowledge if it is about actions and operations by the Serbs. That was my question, not about whether you were afraid at the time, but how you behaved as a witness in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was always interested in the enemy and what they would do. The rest did not interest me. I didn't really choose where to go. I just followed the army. Of course, our army opened fire as well. I have recordings of that kind too. It was trench warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question is about -- you explained to us there was a blockade from the United States when you had channelled your compilations to the United States. Did you personally deal with those who were invited to broadcast your reports?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't invite anyone to do anything. I gave my footage to a Serb emigrant to New Jersey, and later on he told me that none of it was broadcast because nobody wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did he explain to you why that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't really explain. I don't know. For me, it was enough when he said: I really can't find a way to have it broadcast, even if I offer them money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you concluded that this was a blockade, not knowing the reasons why it was refused. Would you agree with me that there may have been -- well, whatever kind of concerns, whether it was sufficiently balanced, sufficiently neutral, sufficiently of quality, that may have caused anyone to not broadcast your compilation. And perhaps I add as a -- yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree to some extent but, really, I don't know. I tried to send footage that was convincing and good. Now, why they refused it, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then one last issue. You said after you had left town, six men entered your apartment. That's found in your statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that statement. It's my neighbour who told me that, the neighbour who lived next door to me and left Bihac later. She said: It is good that you were not there. Six armed men broke into your flat. What they were looking for, I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to your flat, your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go into the apartment, but I did go back to Bihac, and I'm still in touch with my old friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Mr. Jeremy, any questions in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Zoric, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague. I also thank you for the patience you had to have yesterday when we were unfortunately unable to continue with your testimony. I thank you for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Our next witness is Mr. Karac, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then now I'll use the opportunity to briefly deal with the matter I started earlier, which is about the maps. During the testimony of Witness Skrba in June 2014, the Chamber asked the parties to provide the scale of two maps, D526 and P6599, and to identify a number of locations mentioned by the witness on a map. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that the parties agree that the red circles on maps bearing Rule 65 ter number 30976 and 30977 indicate the location of Osmice. These two documents, therefore, can be admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, could you tell us whether you had already reserved a number or whether a number still has to be assigned to these two 65 ter numbers? Well, I've give you time. Just check whether. Meanwhile I continue. The parties have been unable to agree on the location of Gugine Kuce. That's hereby on the record. In relation to P6599, the parties have tentatively agreed that the graphic scale for this map is that one grid equals 2 kilometres. Could the next witness be escorted in the courtroom. The lexical scale is 1 to 50.000. In relation to D526, the Prosecution submits that the lexical scale is 1 to 20.000 but cannot determine on the face of the map the graphic scale. The Defence has not submitted its position. The Chamber invites the parties to file any further agreement related to these matters no later than the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karac. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. In a minute, he will be standing. And Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic who tries to greet you, which he's supposed not to do. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please take care that no loud speaking. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Karac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, please, could you tell us your name slowly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Dragan Karac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, sorry to interrupt for you a second. Mr. Mladic, you should refrain immediately from the kind of communication you're seeking with the public gallery. Therefore, you're invited to not look in that direction. If it happens again, you'll be immediately removed from the courtroom. It may help you if you turn your back to the other direction. No loud speaking either, Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karac, have you given a written statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we display on the screens 1D1664, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The number should be 1D1664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see it on the screen before you, Mr. Karac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's page 1. Do you recognise the signature here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can take a look at the last page. On the last page, do you see the signature? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've had occasion to review this statement. Does it reflect correctly what you've stated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is recorded precisely as I stated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are the contents of this statement truthful and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I've said and described whatever I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would you answer the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender Mr. Karac's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01664 receives Exhibit Number D880, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I would read statement summary of this witness, and we will not have any questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dragan Karac was a JNA reserve officer. He was mobilised in the JNA on the 30th of June, 1991, and joined the 6th Infantry Brigade of Sanski Most. With his unit, he stayed in Jasenovac, Croatia, until 1st April, 1992, after which he was transferred to Sanski Most. The unit was stationed in Lusci Palanka. At the time of his transfer from Jasenovac to Sanski Most, he saw trenches in the Muslim villages along the road towards Sanski Most. He found armed Muslim and Serb groups in and around Sanski Most. The role of his brigade was to keep the peace between the opposing sides. The Muslims were dissatisfied because they had lost the elections, so they took over the municipal building by force, using weapons and renegade police forces composed of Muslims and the Green Berets. SDS recaptured the municipal building with the help of the SOS forces. The members of his brigade did not participate in take-over of the municipal building. For the sake of security of the civilian population, JNA and later VRS units had to disarm the Muslim extremists who were forming check-points from which they killed soldiers and policemen. Mr. Karac was transferred to the 17th Kljuc Brigade in late July 1992. He was engaged at the Bihac front in November 1992. He witnessed that after Bihac was declared a safe area, members of the B and H Army often attacked VRS positions from it. Mr. Karac also participated in combat operations when combined Croatian-Muslim forces carried out an attack on Republika Srpska in August 1995. And that would be, Your Honours, the statement summary of Mr. Karac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karac, no further questions will you put to you by the Defence. Of course, the Chamber has received your statement, so that will be most likely the basis for further examination, because you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You find her to your right. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karac, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it Karac or Karac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: It's a ch at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to mispronounce your name. That's why. I'd like to begin your cross-examination by getting you to confirm a couple of things about the role and the function of an intelligence officer. All right? And I'm going to do that by showing you an excerpt from a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 4643. It's an excerpt from the JNA manual on intelligence support to the armed forces. And we can go over in English to page 16 and B/C/S to page 21, and we're looking for paragraph 11 in both languages. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karac, this paragraph lists - if you can see it okay - the basic intelligence support tasks in war time. And this is specifically relating to brigade-level intel operations because this is excerpted from the JNA brigade rules. All right? So just have a look at some of those tasks. Like 11a talks about -- it says your tasks included the prompt discovering of the actions and intentions of the enemy in the front, in the temporarily occupied territory, and in his rear. And then if in English we could go over to the next page, and have a look at d, you -- part of your job is to collect intel on the combat capability of your enemy. And then in B/C/S over to the next page. E, their movement. F, fire systems -- pardon me, communications, and a couple ones down is fire systems. K, logistics. And go all the way down to n, data about the population and material resources in enemy territory. Now I know this is it at speed, but this isn't a trick question at all. I just want you to confirm that these were among your basic tasks as an intelligence officer; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes. But let me just explain. You said that I was a security officer. That's what you said in your initial remarks. However, at the time, I was assistant commander -- assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence affairs. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think there might have a might misinterpretation because my words specifically spoke about intelligence, and I'm well aware of the divisions between the different branches, so if we could just focus on intel. So can you confirm that these things that we've just listed that you see in paragraph 11 were among your basic tasks as an intel officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that can be confirmed. Those were the rules of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so if we could have that as a Prosecution Exhibit, please, Your Honours, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a very long document, if I -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Only paragraph 11 on pages 16 and 17 in English, and pages 21 and 22 in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And have you made --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you uploaded an excerpt which covers those pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not yet but we can do it forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will reserve a number for an excerpt still to be uploaded. Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7067, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is reserved and we'll wait for the upload to be reported to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be appreciated if you also could upload the cover page so that we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So as an intel officer, your job, your core function really, is to ensure intelligence support for your brigade's combat actions; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, my role was to collect intelligence about the enemy of my army. Of my units, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that involves not only continually monitoring the enemy but also continually assessing the information and continually reporting on it to the people who need to know; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the people who need to know would be particularly the command personnel, the Commander-in-Chief, or Chief of Staff, the operations units, the operations officer, the security officer, among others. Is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: For the most part, what I knew, as far as intelligence was concerned, is what I presented to the Chief of Staff and the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, something else I'd like you just to confirm, and it's about the combat record of your unit and for the moment I just want to focus on the 6th Brigade. And I'll show you a document that reports on your unit's combat records so you can follow along with me as I read it. It's P7015 MFI. And it's a paper from Sanski Most called the "Informator." It's an SDS newspaper and it was published on Petrov Dan, Saint Peter's Day, in 1992. P7015. So that's the first page. And if we go over to pages 38 in English and page 25 in your language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you refresh our memory what day is Saint Peter's Day, so that we also know it, from a calendar point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a saint, the Serbs celebrate that saint, and that day is on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in B/C/S, I think you need to have a look at the third paragraph from the bottom, if I'm not mistaken, on page 25. And when we begin to read, tell me if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And almost the penultimate paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karac, referring to the 6th Infantry Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you make the third paragraph from the bottom, please, a bit bigger for Mr. Karac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This says that your brigade took part in the liberation of Bosanska Krupa; the liberation and mopping up of Hambarine, Kozarusa, and Kozarac; creating conditions for the take-over in Kljuc; confiscation of weapons across the municipality; military defeat of the Muslim extremists in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo; involvement in mopping up all areas on the left bank of Una; involvement in mopping up the areas of Sanica, Krasulje, Hrustovo, and Vrhpolje. Now, up until July 1992, that's right, isn't it, that's an accurate record of your brigade's actions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: As for this information about the activities of the brigade, I know that, but as for the rest, this is the first time I see this SDS bulletin report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you don't disagree with the accuracy of the passage I've read to you in terms of it being an accurate record of your brigade's combat activities up till that point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade - parts of the brigade, not the entire brigade - took part in disarming paramilitary units of the Muslims in these areas that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, more was read to you. It was specific areas, specific activities. Do you disagree with that more detailed description of the operations the brigade had been involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just confirm this part that has to do with the activities of the brigade, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all about the brigade. Could a printout be made -- no, we don't have -- could you read it again. Could you read it again, Ms. Edgerton, so -- and take it step by step to see whether the witness has any reason to disagree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This document says: "The brigade has participated in the following operations: The liberation of Bosanska Krupa." Is that correct, Mr. Karac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying that your brigade didn't take part in the liberation of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, my brigade did not take part in the liberation of Bosanska Krupa. That was this so-called take-over of power.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. We'll come back to that. I'll continue: "The liberation and cleansing of Hambarine, Kozarusa and Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it says in the English translation "mopping up" instead of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- "cleansing."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me. Yes, "the liberation and mopping up," yes, correct. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that your brigade took part in the liberation and mopping up of Hambarine, Kozarusa, and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I know of Hambarine, and I think it was Kozarac, near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I assume you take no issue, because you spoke about it in your written evidence, that your brigade took part in the creation of conditions for the take-over in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, again, since you spoke of it in your written evidence, you can confirm that your brigade took part in the military defeat of Muslim extremists in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade took part in the fighting -- actually, parts of the 6th Brigade took part in the battles for Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, in the disarming of Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "Involving [sic] in mopping up all the areas on the left bank of the Una." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Involvement in mopping up areas of Sanica, Krasulje, Hrustovo, and Vrhpolje." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, it took part in these operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I realise -- I see that this document, P7015, is marked for identification and I don't believe that this page that I've read this excerpt from is included in that exhibit yet. I wonder if it can be added, and then we'll address Your Honours eventually more fully on the complete number of pages we might want to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know whether under that number we have at this moment have an extract or if it's the whole document. Because if it is the whole document, then of course this is part of it as well. But I do understand that you want to make a further selection and that the Defence will be in a position to add whatever they think we would need for contextualising the portions selected by the Prosecution. Therefore, we'll -- it remains to be MFI'd and this then will be part of your selection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karac, you mentioned you actually took issue with the assertion in this document that your brigade had participated in the liberation of Bosanska Krupa. I just want to take this document away and show you another one, then, P3916 [Realtime transcript read in error "P3196"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a document dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please say it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please say it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- apparently there is a -- I don't know what explains it but apparently there's some problem in having "3916" on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the record now, page 43, line 25, we have it correctly there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karac, you've had a chance to have a look at this document. Just go down to the very last paragraph of this document which is dated 11 May 1992 and it's a response to a request and it's directed to the commander of your brigade. So if your brigade, as you say, didn't take part in the liberation of Bosanska Krupa, what's General Talic doing taking this opportunity to pay tribute to and congratulate all the soldiers of your brigade, and the commander personally, for the successfully completed task of liberating the town of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I've already told you that the brigade participated in this so-called take-over of power. That is probably considered to be liberation. I'm not aware of anything else but that. Now, I mean, whether there was something else as well, I cannot confirm that for you. Indeed, this is the first time I'm seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. Just a couple of other details I want to get you to confirm or to maybe augment a little bit your written evidence. You talk about your brigade's arrival in Sanski Most in April 1992. Can you confirm you arrived there with about a thousand men in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for you. I don't think that there were a thousand men in the brigade then when returning from Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, how many do you think there were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I know that approximately -- I mean, the number was growing every day, so the information changed. It's possible that there were a thousand. I don't know. I really don't know. I cannot give you an accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's time for the morning break. I apologise for not noticing that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, we'll keep an eye on the clock. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes when we'll continue. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, two short matters. I think the documents I referred to earlier, that is, 65 ter 30976, no number has been assigned yet. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30976 receives Exhibit Number P7068, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there no objection against it being a P number, admitted into evidence. 30977.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number P7069, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7069 is admitted. Now I'm -- let me just see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Similarly, Your Honours, can I just advise that the excerpts from 65 ter number 4643 have now been uploaded as 4643a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that we reserved a number already.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that number was?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7067, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7067 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just on behalf of my colleague Mr. Jeremy, similarly the excerpts from 65 ter number 31864 have now been uploaded as 31864a, and a provisional number for those was assigned as P7066.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we admitted it already and we instructed Madam Registrar to replace the new -- the old uploaded document by the new one. Therefore there's no need to further decide on the matter and this instruction still stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now informed that it has been uploaded. Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to start up again, Mr. Karac, I'd just like to ask you: Have you ever met General Mladic before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet several -- General Mladic several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was the first time you met General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I think that the first time I met General Mladic was at the Bihac front in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So you've never met with General Mladic before 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect, thank you. Now just to go back to your statement. You said at paragraph 4 on B/C/S page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could show Mr. Karac D880 again. B/C/S page 3. English page 2, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What you said there was -- you talked about the establishment of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly and when the SDS took power in the town. You mentioned some fighting between Serbian representatives and the government. And then you said: "The Muslims were dissatisfied because they had lost the elections, so they took over the municipal building by force, using weapons and renegade forces composed of Muslims and Green Berets." So when you refer to the Muslims losing the elections, are you -- do we understand you right that you're talking about the multi-party elections in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
