utterances.text: Yes, that's when the SDS had a majority, at those elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that because the SDS won the elections about -- more than a year earlier, the Muslims took over the municipality building in April 1992; right? Because that's what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, they took the municipality building and that's where they stayed and they didn't want to leave. The Serb representatives of government could not enter the building, the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you missed the gist of the question. The question was whether it was because they had lost the elections, that that is what is explains that more than one and a half year later they took control of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really wouldn't know what the motives were of the Muslim representatives, why they were in the building of the municipal assembly then, and why they didn't allow the Serb representatives to enter the municipality building. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time, your statement suggests that it was because they had lost the elections, where it reads: "The Muslims were dissatisfied because they had lost the elections, so they took over the municipal building by force ..." That suggests that that's the reason why. Listen carefully to the next question that Ms. Edgerton will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the fact that the non-Serb police had been dispossessed of the SUP on the order of the municipality president, Nedeljko Rasula, had nothing do with the Muslim move into the municipality building. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I really can't confirm. I just don't have any relevant facts to explain it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, were you -- were you there in the town of Sanski Most at the time that this happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: No, I was not in Sanski Most. The command of my brigade was in Luska Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you say that Muslims took over the municipal building by force, that's not because you saw any of it at all; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I didn't see it, really. That's something I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you said in paragraph 5 of your written evidence that: "The members of my brigade did not participate in occupying the municipal building," is that also something you didn't see but you only heard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I know, and I heard, where different parts of my brigade were located. I know for a fact they did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then you would know for a fact that what they did do was secure the area all around the municipality building and other local institutions to allow for other forces, Serb forces, to take them over.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I want to show you another document. It's P3294. It's the diary of Mr. Rasula, who I just spoke about. And in this diary he has noted a lot of discussions and minutes and decisions that were taken by members of the Crisis Staff that he was a member of around this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to English page 19 and B/C/S page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the page in your language, Mr. Karac, I want you to go on the right-hand side and just have a look at the top of the page on the right-hand side. There's a heading there that says: "Course of action in taking over power and establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most." And right below it, there's a date, and it says 14 April. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it refers after that to a session of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party being held on that day, and a number of things being decided. And the decisions are on the page that are in -- that's in front of you in your language but we'll need to go over to the next page to look at those decisions. So, in English, they're at the top of the page, numbers 1 to 4. And you see them, too. The decisions are to conclude negotiations with the SDA about the division of the municipality, that police forces declare their loyalty to the Serb republic and acceptance of Serbian symbols and insignia, and that any possibility of opposition or intervention on behalf of the adversary be thwarted. If we go to the bottom of the page that your language --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we need to go to the top of the page 17 in B/C/S and on to page 21 in -- sorry, no, stay on page -- the present page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see that -- the notation that: Security measures to forestall any resistance by the opposite side are given below. And then if we go over to point number 2 in English - next page - the security measures are set out. A platoon of reservists from the 6th Krajina Brigade are going to secure and control the bridge, the square, the park, the municipal building, and the post office. And then further, at b there's some tasks for the police that are set out, and at c, some tasks fort Territorial Defence units. Now, you agreed that your job as an intel officer was to keep your command organs constantly updated on the situation. Now, three days before the Muslims even entered the Sanski Most building, five days before the forces that you don't know anything about attacked it, here's a detailed plan for the Serb take-over of Sanski Most involving forces of your brigade. So you must have been a very bad intelligence officer if you didn't know anything about this plan for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it says that this was enforced, and is it the position of the Prosecution that the Crisis Staff was commanding by JNA units at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a mixed objection and comment. If there's any problem with putting a text to the witness, Ms. Edgerton, if there's any dispute about that, please read to him exactly what you wanted to draw his attention to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I have done that, with respect, Your Honours. I've read everything that I've wanted the witness to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, then, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify. My objection was: Is there any proof that this was enforced or this is only on the paper of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's a question. That's a question which, of course, does not need to appear from the document. It is -- if you say you write a book, the question is did you sell it, that means that, of course, the book itself wouldn't tell you that it was sold. It's just a question. There's no reason to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the question is about the knowledge about this plan for action, about this plan, not about enforcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton asked whether this gentleman agrees that it was his job as intelligence officer to keep his command organs constantly updated on the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the question. Look at the last two lines of her question: "So you must have been very bad intelligence officer if you didn't know anything about this plan for action."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is denied. May that be clear. Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to -- I'm trying to find the cite on the transcript where the gentleman, Mr. Karac, discussed his basic tasks in war time. If I could just have a moment, just to make things perhaps a bit easier, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karac, you confirmed at temporary transcript page 39 that your role was to collect intelligence about the enemy of your army, of your units. And then my question was: "And that involves not only continually monitoring the enemy but also continually assessing the information and continually reporting on it to people who need to know; right?" And you said: "Yes." So given that answer, I'd like you to have a think about the question I asked about this plan of action. If this was your job, how can you claim you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. It should be established first whether his job was to monitor Crisis Staff. Was it an enemy? I don't understand at all how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- those two could be connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not -- we're not discussing at this moment the questions, neither are we discussing the meaning of those words. You can do that in re-examination. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this gentleman was intelligence officer, not security officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I said the objection is denied, Mr. Lukic. That's a ruling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Mr. Karac, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I really don't know about these tasks of the Crisis Staff. How would I? Now, whether a platoon of reservists of the 6th Krajina Brigade protected and controlled the bridge on the Sana river, I don't know. The commander probably decided to protect the safety of his unit. Because it was quite to be expected at the time that the enemy would try to destroy the bridge. I don't know whether it was really in the context of the Crisis Staff as the text says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's just flip over to page 22 in English. A meeting started on 20 April 1992, and I'll try to find the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I think it's page 18 -- no, 22 in B/C/S, I think. 21. Please go one page back to the page bearing the number R1091614. Now, if it takes too long, I'll come back to it after our break, Your Honour, so we can move on and take advantage of the time, but I will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to move on, Mr. Karac, to talk about the disarming operations you -- you discuss in your written evidence. You talked about two locations, Mahala and Hrustovo. First of all, you would agree with me that Mahala is a Muslim suburb of the town of Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's a residential area. People lived there before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, in your statement, in your written evidence, at paragraph 11, you talked about -- you talked in more detail about Mahala and you said you weren't present when Mahala was disarmed. Where were you in May 1992 during the course of the operation against Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where I was at that time. But when I was talking about that and saying that I was not present during the mopping up of Mahala, I meant that I was not physically there. Now where I was, I really can't remember now. Maybe I was in a different part of the front line or something. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if you weren't physically there, how do you know that the army issued a call to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: More than once the brigade command issued appeals for people to surrender their weapons, and they set deadlines. A number of Muslims surrendered their weapons; others didn't. And then the disarming operation began.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't quite answer my question. I asked how you knew.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I knew because there was talk about it in the brigade command. Every time an operation was finished, people discussed how it had developed and what had been going on that day in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you heard those radio announcements that you specifically referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would know that those -- there wasn't just one, there wasn't just two, but the call to surrender by the army was continuous. It was going on all the time. You would know that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know how many times the announcement was made at Radio Sanski Most. But, yes, they were made. I heard them several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get some clarification from the witness. Witness, you just said that you heard about this call to surrender because it was being discussed after the operation; people were talking about it in the brigades. Now, you say you heard the announcements being made. Which of the two is actually correct? Did you hear the announcements, or did you hear from discussions after the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, both are true. I heard announcements on the radio, on the one hand; and on other hand, I got more information in the brigade command after operations were completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So having heard some of those radio announcements, you would have heard the broadcasts that Sanski Most was a Serbian town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the witness does not receive interpretation. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The translator cannot turn on his microphone, I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it seems that the -- I see from the red light that the microphone is functional again. I'll switch off my microphone. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Still the microphone of the interpreters' booth is not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for a technician to resolve the problem and we should have some patience.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I have it now again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So had you -- if you'd heard those broadcasts -- oh, still nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's again not working.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How frustrating for our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked already but I think there are no unnecessary microphones open.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unfortunate that no technicians have arrived yet -- oh, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that a technician was at the door-step of the booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the functioning of the microphone is on and off. I now see that it is functioning. I'll switch off my microphone. If after that you would switch on yours, Ms. Edgerton, then we perhaps have a chance of success.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, is there any way you could use another socket or other microphone? Because it may -- your microphone may interfere with the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The technician should stay in the booth until the problem is resolved fully.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not, I believe, in our booth. It's somewhere else. So we will have to see where exactly it is, and the technician needs to go and see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Having heard these radio announcements -- my --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karac still can't hear me speak in his own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would have heard then that Sanski Most was a Serbian town and people were being called on to hand over their weapons or face destruction. You would have heard that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I knew that Sanski Most was not a Serbian place. I knew that Muslims lived in Sanski Most. In what percentage, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, did you hear that people were being called on to hand over their weapons voluntarily or face destruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I never heard appeals to kill or destroy people. I heard about surrendering weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility that it happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I can't rule out that possibility, Your Honours. It might have happened, but if it did, it was only individual cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there may be some confusion. You were asked about whether you heard the announcement on the radio. Then you were asked whether you then also heard that it was broadcasted that people were called on to hand over their weapons voluntarily or face destruction. You said you never heard appeals of this kind. And then when you answered the question about whether you could exclude the possibility that it happened, "it" not being very clear, but apparently Ms. Edgerton referring to the use of this language in the calls made by the radio, you answered: "It might have happened, but if it did, it was only individual cases." The question simply is: When listening to these call-ups, did you hear the threatening language as was put to you by Ms. Edgerton? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the appeal by the brigade command, one part of the population left the area. So one part of the weaponry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what -- no, that's not what I'm asking. I'm asking whether you heard this language that they would face destruction if they would not hand over their weapons. Did you hear that language being broadcasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that members of the Army of Republika Srpska would disarm these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apparently for one reason or another, you don't want to address the question I put to you. Did you hear that when people were called up to hand over their weapons, that it was added that if they would not voluntarily do so, that they would face destruction. Did you hear that as part of the announcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who did not hand in their weapons were a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apparently the witness is not answering my question, for one reason or another. Therefore, this will affect, of course, the probative value of his evidence. Last time: Did you hear, when you listened to the broadcast, that where they were invited to hand over their weapons, that if they would not voluntarily do so, that they would have to face - what was it? - destruction? Did you hear that to be said on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot now give you the exact quotation of the radio announcement, but I can confirm from the military point of view that armed people for us were legitimate targets to destroy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we're not talking about targets. We are talking about what was broadcasted. Now, you said you don't remember exactly. Can you exclude that such language was used over the radio when people were called upon to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really couldn't say any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I noticed, Mr. Karac, in your statement that when you talked about Mahala, you omitted to mention that units of your brigade shelled Mahala after the radio announcements that we're talking about, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You omitted to mention, when talking about Mahala, that units of your brigade shelled it after the radio announcements we're talking about. You omitted it; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I know there was shelling, and from what I heard from my colleagues at the command, the shells did not land on the inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're confirming now that units of the 6th Brigade, your brigade, shelled Mahala; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's exactly the opposite what the witness already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the witness only said that they did not land on the inhabited area. Now, that's -- again, you can further explore that matter in re-examination. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to be precise. It's -- we're talking about units of the 6th Brigade that shelled; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a couple of shells that fell, but I repeat: The shells did not land on the inhabited area. They did not fall on buildings. It was more of a warning to people to hand in their weapons, to disarm paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of the fact that civilians were killed in Mahala as a result of this shelling, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't have such information. Or, rather, I don't know about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You know, however, that your brigade, units of your brigade, entered Mahala after this shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, units entered Mahala after that shelling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- and as intel officer you would also know that once your units entered Mahala, they arrested people in huge numbers; right? You know that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, some of these people were arrested, and that was done by the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, the numbers arrested were extraordinary. There was around 2.000 civilians who were taken out of Mahala once units of your brigade had entered; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I know that before the operation -- well, I don't know what the exact number is, but I know that before the operation, a certain number, and there were several hundreds civilians that had left the area, I mean, Mahala ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you're the intel officer, so your job is to get intelligence on enemy activities for your units, and one of the ways you do that is by interrogating people that your forces had detained. So you -- you can't tell us how many people were arrested following the take-over of Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honours. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But I put the number to you of around 2.000 people. That's a huge logistical concern. You would have had to mobilise resources to conduct the interrogations you needed to do to brief your commander, and you now don't know how many people came into your custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Again there is mixing between intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no mixing --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton said "you" -- she should first ask this gentleman whether he interrogated anybody and whether it was his job, whether it was his duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's suggested and that is permissible in cross-examination. You may suggest these kind of things. That's what we call leading questions. And if you disagree, then you can re-visit the matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was without foundation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is what is allowed in cross-examination. Please try to understand the difference. Of course, there's no basis for it. You suggest something to a witness and then you ask the witness to confirm or not, and that's exactly the difference. But we may have noticed that earlier that you're not fully aware of what the difference is between examination-in-chief in which leading questions are not allowed, where a basis has to be laid, compared to leading questions in cross-examination. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is your answer that you were not aware of this huge number of people being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the number, but I know that people had been arrested, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you have no idea whether it was 2, or 500, or 10.000? You had no idea about how many had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said, Your Honour, that I don't know the exact number, whether it was 50, 100, 150, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then give us the approximate number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't want to say anything that was not true. Believe me, I don't know exactly what number it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were to say anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that Ms. Edgerton has difficulties in understanding that you, in your position, had no knowledge whatsoever about numbers, where, as she suggests to you, it would have had perhaps quite an impact on the job you were doing. That's the issue. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to finish up with Mahala, Mr. Karac, in fact, the operation to mop up, to disarm the settlement of Mahala was a planned and co-ordinated operation that didn't only touch on that area but a number of non-Serb areas. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the situation was. And as for all of these activities that were being carried out, they had all been planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. And the operation was so effective and the devastation in Mahala was so serious that the situation was actually used as -- as a threat for remaining Muslim-held areas, wasn't it? People were given the choice: Surrender or face the same situation that Mahala did.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I don't know how Muslims understood it at that point. Probably that way, but I really don't know. I mean, whether they understood our action then as some kind of a threat so that others would do -- well, later on, it turned out that it wasn't that way. According to some information, part of these people from Mahala withdrew towards Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. Now what the number was, I really don't know. However, people were saying that between 150 and 200 people returned to Vrhpolje and Golaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mr. Karac, this Chamber has received the recordings of the radio broadcasts we've been discussing, and, in fact, the -- there was nothing unclear about the message to the Muslims, and I want to have a look at one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P3301, please. Now, I want to go to B/C/S page 3 and English page 3, in fact. And in -- hmm. Your indulgence for a moment. Apologies. Could we go to 3302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have the feeling that you were looking at the English part. It's on top of the page which is currently on the screen, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For another purpose. And I'm not able to find the B/C/S immediately. But perhaps we could go to 3302 and I have the -- mm-hm. And, again, your indulgence for a moment. Let's go to English page 7 and B/C/S page 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct you to the commentary by the female voice which begins on page 7 and runs over to page 8. But what this woman says to the people who are listening to the broadcast is that: "Your resistance will force us to destroy and devastate your villages which means that you will not be able to live with us in these territories. And if you" --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have to go over to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "If you do want to go on living with us in these territories, accept co-operation and hand over all the weapons and military equipment and surrender to the Serbian authorities all the extremists who force to you fight." And then there's a list of villages a little bit further down the page who are called to surrender their weapons. And -- among them Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. But at the very sentence following that list of names, there's one more reminder to the non-Serbs: "Again, we call on you to be sensible and ask the inhabitants to respond to this call. If not, we will be forced to act as we did with Mahala." So, Mr. Karac, the message was very clear: The choice was to surrender and pledge allegiance to a mono-ethnic Serbian authority or face destruction. That was the choice the non-Serbs at Sanski Most had to make, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: The Muslim population kept part of the -- actually, part of the paramilitary formations kept their weapons and uniforms, and they had clashed with the Army of Republika Srpska. The Army of Republika Srpska responded to this provocation or, rather, disarmed these paramilitary formations. Now, I mean, whether they had a choice. Well, probably. I mean, to hand over their weapons and to leave as free citizens or to clash. We all know what an armed clash entails and what the consequences of an armed clash are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is an armed clash automatically that villages will be destroyed and devastated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends, Your Honour, on the intensity of combat and what kind of enemy is there. So if the enemy is better fortified, then targets will be selected. So it's not the same when one uses heavy weaponry and artillery or just side-arms. That's the intensity that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not what the broadcast says. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's time for the next break, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber takes it when you said that this morning you complained when you were at the Registry that it was not a complaint against the Registry. Not them to blame for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not complaint about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's how --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the Registry. It's about our database, about our records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not complaint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's well understood. That's hereby on the record. And then rather than to express your problems to the Registry perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I created any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you have organised your team well, then even you don't have to inform the Registry about your concerns. We leave it to that. There was one other matter. You intervened when Ms. Edgerton was asking questions about what was ordered and you said, well, he is an intelligence officer not a security officer, which suggests that the logic and the formal definitions are always guiding. Again, you can explore that in re-examination. But if I see that the Municipal Board of a party decides on how to instruct the army, then perhaps the formal lines are not always as clear as in practice. Therefore, again, no problem with examining the witness on that but it was not a reason to intervene in this specific context. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karac, just to finish up with Mahala. Just before we broke, you were explaining to Judge Orie about the intensity of combat and what kind of enemy is there, and made the observation that if the enemy is better fortified, then targets would be selected. But just bringing that whole discussion back to Mahala, in fact, any forces that might have been, any Bosnian forces that might have been in Mahala were completely outmatched by the strength of your unit and their weaponry. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the position of the Prosecution that there were Bosnian army soldiers in Mahala at the time? Or is it just a supposition, a hypothetical question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not able to give Your Honours an immediate answer on this, but I'll be able to do that forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if could you indulge me for a moment, I seem to have plugged into some non-working microphones in here and I would like to be able to just take full part in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is move on to another area you talked about in your written evidence and that's about the disarming, because that's what you called it, of Hrustovo. Now Hrustovo is another Muslim area of Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, once again, when you refer to "the army," like you did at paragraph 13 of your written evidence, and I'll read you exactly what you said. You said: "When the army approached Hrustovo in combat formation just before it entered Hrustovo, the army came under fire, and when the army was attacked there was an exchange of fire," and so forth. So here when you refer to "the army," do you mean again to refer to units of your brigade, the 6th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, I meant that, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you discussed Hrustovo, what I also noticed was you omitted to mention -- you omitted to mention that 1st -- soldiers of your brigade, 1st Infantry Brigade soldiers, went in and killed women and children who had taken refuge inside a garage in Hrustovo. You omitted that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Had I known, I would have said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge about the fact that soldiers of your unit stood in front of the garage and opened up with automatic machine-guns and threw hand-grenades into the garage and killed civilians. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question again. In cross-examination you can sometimes put a question twice. Please proceed. Did you -- did you -- your evidence is that you had no knowledge about what was described by Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know, I mean, but I don't rule out the possibility that that did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also never learned later that that may have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't interested in that. I was involved in a different unit so that stayed that way, unresolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Hrustovo is the one place where you were actually personally on scene, right? Because that's what we can understand from your written evidence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I was not on the actual front line with the soldiers. I was part of the brigade command. Because, at that time, as far as I can remember, I was in Tomina, in the village of Tomina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'd look to move to another area and it's actually the final area. And I want to do that, I want to start telling you about an event on 14 May 1992. Now, on that day in Kljuc, there was a big political military meeting. And General Galic was there, your commander, Basara was there, and there were municipal heads from all the municipalities covered by a larger area that represented the area of responsibility of the 30th Infantry Division. Now, at that meeting, all the participants were briefed about the strategic objectives that had been announced by President Karadzic at the Bosnian Serb Assembly two days previously. And you know about that meeting, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's because you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so since you were there, you can confirm that -- actually, I'll do this another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look, then, at 65 ter number 31874.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How big was the meeting? And where was it held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I think it was held in the building of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc where I was present, myself, for a while. Part of that meeting, that is. Since Colonel Basara took me along, since I am from Kljuc, so that I could see my family at the same time. So that is the reason why I was in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's go over in the B/C/S which happens to be on the left-hand side, although what you see is in English, over to, I think, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you see in front of you is a JNA military notebook. And you're familiar with these, aren't you? Every officer had one of these; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they're --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They're official books; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes. Official books that every officer had and the number of pages was certified on the last page, and then these notebooks were returned to the organ that they had originally been received from. When it is completed, then the notebook has to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is your notebook, isn't it? That's your name in your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go over in this B/C/S book to pages -- page 66. And we don't actually need to move at all in English. But perhaps you can enlarge the right-hand side of page 66 so Mr. Karac can see his own notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karac, here's your notes of the meeting that you were at. Actually, you have it noted as being the 13th of July, 1995, and not the 14th. And you listed the persons present, including Colonel Galic, Colonel Basara, and representatives of the municipalities of Kljuc and Mrkonjic Grad and Jajce. Now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I missed Sipovo. So just because you haven't seen this, I would imagine, in quite a few years, I'd actually like to give you a moment to have a look at your own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to the next page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like Mr. Karac to have a look at both sides, again, just so that can he see what his notes say on the first page, and then go over to the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Could you please make it larger? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here's the military giving some briefings on the situation, including your Colonel Basara. And you could just tell us when you get to the bottom of your page that you've got presently displayed in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: We can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So here you've got notes of seven strategic goals. These were the goals that you were told had been announced at the meeting in Banja Luka, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the goals that were notified to us then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these are ... these were your war goals, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Those were not my war goals. Those were the goals set by the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could we just go quickly over to another document and then we'll come back to this one. P2867.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here we've got some minutes of that same meeting that you took such good notes of, listing the same participants. And if you go over to page 3 in both languages, setting out at points 1 to 6, almost the same strategic goals. Now, I know it's going fast, but if we can hop over to page 4 in both languages, I want to draw your attention to something General Galic said. And if you need to, I can go back to the immediately preceding page so you can see, you can confirm for yourself that it is attributed to General Galic; but if not, I want to draw your attention to the first bullet point -- I'm speaking about the English version. I want to draw your attention to the first bullet point underneath General Galic's proposal for a conclusion. General Galic says: "Implement the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka but submit them to the commands of units and municipalities." So here's my question that I'd like you to confirm: In the area of responsibility of your brigade, this is how co-operation as between the different arms of authority happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the strategic goals that were set in Banja Luka were shared goals that guided your military operations. That's what this document shows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: They were not shared goals. They came down from the state leadership, and the army was supposed to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, in fact, when you said -- can we just go back to the preceding page and we can look at the first goal again, which you also have noted in your notebook. So when you said in your written evidence that the role of your brigade wasn't -- was to keep the peace between the opposing sides, that's actually incorrect, isn't it, because the first overarching goal of your brigade and the military forces was to ensure a state separation of three national communities; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is misrepresenting the evidence she just pulled up. On the screen, we don't have it, but the last page we had a moment ago, and we should see what Galic - Mr. Galic at the time, probably not General yet - said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what Madam Edgerton is quoting at this moment is number one on the page that is before us. Is there anything wrong with that quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question is in contradiction with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then re-read the question. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- I asked you to ... the objection is denied. I will give you in detail the reasons why. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give it to me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will give it at a -- before you have an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I not object when somebody is misrepresenting the evidence that it's addressing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is not the beginning of a debate. This is a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I said that the reasons will follow soon in more detail but I'm not inclined to do that in the presence of the witness at this moment. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'm going to do is actually maybe to help Mr. Karac and go back to his diary for a second at 65 ter number 31874, having seen this document. And in B/C/S, I want to go to page 68, I think, and English page 3. Make it English page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what happened, Mr. Karac, after this meeting was that you and the staff held a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We could go -- we should go and enlarge the right-hand side of the B/C/S page of Mr. Karac's notebook. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the 14th of May in 1992, so the next day after this meeting, there was a brigade command meeting. And do you see the citation that says "General Mladic" and then lists a number of points below that: To close geographic latitudes so that borders can be defended successfully. It has been envisaged that those territories are compact. And then you might be able to read the next passage better for us because it's in your handwriting and I think the translator has missed a word. "Europe," with a question mark, "has envisaged relocation also," and then it goes on. Point number 1. So I asked you at the beginning -- here's my question. I asked about -- at the beginning of the second session you were here whether you had met General Mladic before and you said only in 1994. So General Mladic wasn't here at this meeting, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't see that before me. I don't know which document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Have a look, the screen in front of you, underneath the title that you've underlined where it says: "Meeting of the brigade command and the battalion commander." There's a small notation, just at the top on the left-hand side, and it says "General Mladic." If you don't see that, you can still answer the question. General Mladic wasn't at this meeting, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: General Mladic was not present at that meeting. Why I wrote "General Mladic," I really can't remember now. Maybe somebody talked about General Mladic or something, but I maintain that General Mladic was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't think so, but let me put this to you. Here's what I think is happening at this meeting. So four days after the strategic objectives are announced by Dr. Karadzic in Banja Luka, they're briefed to the political -- the Serbian political and military leaders in your area, and then the following day, here you were receiving even more detailed instructions from Mladic's subordinates about different aspects of those war goals. That's what was going on; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you maybe put it differently?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. You heard the war goals. You were at the meeting where they were discussed. The next day, the whole brigade command had a meeting with their battalion commanders about those war goals and how they should be implemented, and that's what you noted on the 14th of May, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So I asked you a little while ago about the first objective, and we can go back to that page in your notebook so you yourself can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's page 66, so it's the page immediately preceding. 67, pardon me. And I think it's page 2 in the translated version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So have a look again at goal number 1 that you noted down. Goal number 1 is: "State separation from the other two communities." So I want to put to you is: Based on what you said, your brigade's task had nothing -- based on what you said and what happened in Sanski Most, your brigade's task had nothing to do with keeping the peace between the factions. It was to ensure their separation pursuant to the war goals articulated by the Bosnian Serb leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I said the brigade had arrived in the area of Sanski Most to keep peace in the municipality, and that was indeed done until the moment when attacks began against members of the army of what was then the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Until then, they were keeping the peace. However, when the members of the army were attacked, the army responded, and then these orders followed and we received well-defined, strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in places -- just going to the two places you spoke about in your written evidence, Mahala and Hrustovo, by the 30th of May, 1992, there were no non-Serbs left, were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC
utterances.text: I think that was so. I believe the majority of the population had already left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll have nothing further, Your Honours. And what I'm going to ask is for the selected pages that we discussed about 65 ter 31874 to be admitted and as a Prosecution Exhibit, and we'll upload those excerpts forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll wait for that selection. Meanwhile we should reserve a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives P7070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, could you tell us how much time would you approximately need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to calculate. Probably 15 minutes. Not more than 20, 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll have to do that tomorrow. Perhaps it's better also then to start your re-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll adjourn soon but you are already -- you may go already. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning for only a very short session at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom. And I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. You may follow the usher. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence. I've been beckoned by Mr. Tieger. And just with respect to the query by your colleague His Honour Judge Moloto, if I may I'd like to come back to Your Honours with a response to that first thing tomorrow morning when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, I think I still owe you the reasoning for the denial of your objection. I carefully read the question. The first part of the question is about the first goal, as it appears in the notebook, and then the question followed by: "So when you said in your written evidence that the role of your brigade was to keep the peace between opposing sides, that's actually incorrect ..." I think that's what the statement says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then it continued by saying: "... because the first overarching goal of your brigade and the military forces was to ensure state separation of the three national communities." And that is what is found, I think, in the document we had read; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the continuation but the question was composed that Ms. Edgerton wanted to show that this witness is not telling the truth when he said that the goal of the brigade was to separate warring parties at that time. And the document we saw on our screens exactly said the same, and using that document to prove the opposite is not logical for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, whether it's logical or not, that is something different from misrepresenting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was misrepresentation of the evidence as well. Because the document said differently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what Ms. Edgerton did with this question and why I ruled that the objection was denied is that she put opposite to each other the statement of the witness compared to what is found in the document as the first strategic goal as written down in that notebook. There's nothing wrong with that because it's fully understandable that one reads that as possibly inconsistent, the one with the other, and that's what Ms. Edgerton referred to in her question and that's the reason why I ruled that the objection was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will deal with that tomorrow in my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No problem to deal with such matters in re-examination, Mr. Lukic, I emphasise that again and again. Therefore, we'll wait and hear tomorrow. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 28th of January, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of January, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
